references.text: The day before, John the Baptist had pointed to Jesus and said: "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!" ([ref:Joh 1:29|John 1:29]). In verse 36 he repeats the core of this testimony – "Ἴδε ὁ ἀμνὸς τοῦ θεοῦ" – in a shortened form to two of his disciples, without the addition about taking away the sin of the world.

The Passover lamb in [ref:2 Mos 12:3-6|Exodus 12:3-6] is a fundamental background for the image of "the Lamb of God." The lamb was to be without blemish and was slaughtered as an offering for the people's deliverance from judgment in Egypt.

The prophecy about the Lord's suffering servant in [ref:Jes 53:7|Isaiah 53:7] describes him as a lamb led to slaughter, and as a sheep that is silent before its shearers. This text underlies John's identification of Jesus as "the Lamb of God."

Peter writes that believers are redeemed "with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot" ([ref:1 Pet 1:18-19|1 Peter 1:18-19]). This confirms the New Testament understanding of Jesus as the perfect sacrificial lamb.

In [ref:Åp 5:6|Revelation 5:6] John sees in his vision a Lamb standing as though it had been slain, right before the throne. The Lamb as an image of the crucified and risen Christ is a central theme in Revelation, directly continuing from John the Baptist's testimony.
In [ref:Åp 5:12|Revelation 5:12] the heavenly host sings: "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain." This shows the final exaltation of the Lamb of God whom John the Baptist pointed to.

Philip preached the gospel about Jesus based on Isaiah 53, where the Ethiopian official read about him being "led like a lamb to the slaughter" ([ref:Apg 8:32-35|Acts 8:32-35]). The early church understood Jesus as the fulfillment of the prophecy concerning God's sacrificial Lamb.

The two disciples heard John's testimony about the Lamb of God and followed Jesus ([ref:Joh 1:37|John 1:37]). The testimony in verse 36 had an immediate effect, leading the first disciples to begin following Jesus.

Paul writes: "For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" ([ref:1 Kor 5:7|1 Corinthians 5:7]). This directly links Jesus to the sacrificial function of the Passover lamb and confirms the theological significance of calling Jesus "the Lamb of God."
